    Choose your entry

    Start with the route that matches your education and career stage. Always confirm age, medical and stream eligibility in the active notice.

    NDA & Naval Academy

    The officer-entry route after Class 12. The written exam has Mathematics and the General Ability Test, followed by SSB and medical examination.

    • Written paperMaths 300 + GAT 600
    • Duration2½ hours each
    • Questions120 Maths + 150 GAT
    • InterviewSSB: 900 marks
    • Penalty⅓ of question marks

    What to prioritise

    Maths: algebra, matrices, trigonometry, coordinate geometry, calculus, vectors, statistics and probability.

    GAT: English (200) plus physics, chemistry, general science, history, geography and current events (400).

    Army wing requires Class 12; Navy, Air Force and INAC routes require the science/PCM conditions stated in the notification.

    Combined Defence Services

    Graduate officer entry for IMA, INA, AFA and OTA. IMA/INA/AFA candidates write English, GK and Elementary Mathematics; OTA candidates write English and GK.

    • IMA / INA / AFA3 × 100 marks
    • OTA2 × 100 marks
    • Duration2 hours per paper
    • After writtenSSB + medical

    Best use of time

    Build accuracy in English and arithmetic first: these improve through daily drills. Keep GK revision short but frequent. For OTA, use the saved mathematics block for extra English and current-affairs practice.

    Degree and subject requirements differ by academy. AFA and INA have specific degree/10+2 conditions; check the active UPSC notice.

    Air Force Common Admission Test

    • Online test100 questions / 300 marks
    • Duration2 hours
    • Scoring+3 correct · −1 wrong
    • SectionsGA, English, Maths, Reasoning
    • Next stageAFSB + medical

    Branch lens

    Flying: numerical speed, spatial reasoning and a calm AFSB performance matter.

    Ground Duty: technical and non-technical branches have different degree criteria.

    Technical: verify whether the current notice includes any separate technical testing or branch-specific qualification.

    AFCAT rules can change by cycle. Treat the active IAF notification as final.

    Army Agniveer

    Category-specific online Common Entrance Examination, followed by recruitment rally stages, document checks and medical examination.

    • General Duty50 questions / 100
    • Technical50 questions / 200
    • Clerk / Store Keeper50 questions / 200
    • Core subjectsGK, science, maths, reasoning

    Category strategy

    GD: broad accuracy across GK, science and maths.

    Technical: physics, chemistry and mathematics carry the load.

    Clerk/SKT: English is the largest block; computer basics and part-wise qualifying rules matter.

    Question mix and qualifying requirements vary by category.

    Navy Agniveer SSR / MR

    • SSR100 questions / 60 min
    • SSR subjectsEnglish, science, maths, GA
    • MR50 questions / 30 min
    • MR subjectsScience & maths, GA
    • Penalty0.25 per wrong answer

    Sea-service preparation

    For SSR, practise one-minute questions: the paper rewards immediate recall and clean calculation. For MR, revise Class 10 science and arithmetic in mixed sets. Both routes require physical and medical qualification.

    The 2026 pattern also includes SSR (Medical), with English, science, biology and general awareness.

    Air Force Agniveervayu

    Phase-I is an objective, bilingual online test (except English). Paper length depends on the chosen subject stream.

    • SciencePhysics, maths, English · 60 min
    • Other than scienceEnglish + RAGA · 45 min
    • Both streamsAll sections · 85 min
    • Penalty0.25 per wrong answer

    What follows

    Shortlisted candidates move to document verification, physical fitness, adaptability tests and medical examination. Science candidates should work from 10+2 physics and mathematics; non-science candidates should prioritise English, reasoning and general awareness.

    Selection map

    Different entries vary, but the journey usually follows this sequence.

    01Written / online testAccuracy, speed, syllabus coverage and smart question selection.
    02ScreeningSSB Stage I or service-specific shortlisting and document verification.
    03AssessmentSSB/AFSB tasks, rally fitness or adaptability tests, depending on entry.

    Agreement

    • Each, every, either, neither take a singular verb: “Each cadet is ready.”
    • With either…or / neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
    • “A number of” takes plural; “the number of” takes singular.
    • Collective nouns are singular when the group acts as one unit.

    Tense control

    • Use simple past for a finished time: “The unit arrived yesterday.”
    • Use present perfect for an unfinished period or present result.
    • In reported speech, backshift when the reporting verb is past—unless the fact remains universally true.
    • After “did,” use the base verb: “did not go,” never “did not went.”

    • 1857: widespread uprising; Crown rule followed in 1858.

    Geography anchors

    • Southwest monsoon has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches.
    • Himalayan rivers are largely perennial; Peninsular rivers depend more on rainfall.
    • Black soil suits cotton; alluvial soil dominates northern plains.
    • Coriolis effect deflects moving air right in Northern Hemisphere.

    Defence literacy

    • Know service commands, ranks, training academies and tri-service organisations.
    • Track major exercises by countries involved and service type—not just names.
    • For current affairs, record event, actors, location, purpose and one strategic implication.
    • Revise official updates monthly; dated current affairs cannot remain “current” forever.

    Series & analogy

    • Check first differences, then second differences, ratios and alternating terms.
    • For letters, map A=1…Z=26 and test shifts.
    • In analogies, name the relation before viewing options.
    • For odd-one-out, identify the rule shared by exactly three items.

    Coding & directions

    • Test direct shifts, reverse alphabet, pair swaps and word reversal.
    • Draw direction questions on a coordinate cross; never solve mentally.
    • Facing north: right=east, left=west. Rotate the frame after every turn.
    • Net displacement uses Pythagoras only after horizontal and vertical totals.

    Syllogism discipline

    • “All A are B” does not mean “all B are A.”
    • “Some” means at least one, not all.
    • Two negative premises produce no valid conclusion.
    • Use simple Venn circles; accept only conclusions forced in every valid diagram.

    Spatial reasoning

    • For paper folding, unfold in reverse order and mirror each fold.
    • Opposite faces on a cube never meet along an edge.
    • Count rotations by tracking one fixed reference feature.
    • In embedded figures, ignore orientation and scale unless specified.

    1. Mathematics: Algebra, Trigonometry, Calculus & Statistics

    Mathematics carries the heaviest single-paper weight in defence exams: NDA Paper-I is 300 marks (120 questions, 2.5 hours), CDS Elementary Mathematics is 100 questions, AFCAT's numerical ability is roughly 18 questions, and Agniveer GD/Ck papers test Class-X-level maths. The syllabus is finite and repeats: master the formulas below — and the traps examiners set around them.

    Algebra

    Quadratic equations. For ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), roots are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides the nature of roots: D > 0 → two real distinct roots; D = 0 → two equal real roots; D < 0 → a pair of complex conjugate roots (non-real). Sum of roots = −b/a, product = c/a. Trap: if coefficients are real and one root is 2 + 3i, the other is 2 − 3i — complex roots of real-coefficient quadratics always occur in conjugate pairs.

    Complex numbers. z = a + ib, i² = −1. Modulus |z| = √(a² + b²); conjugate z̄ = a − ib; and z·z̄ = |z|². Powers of i cycle every 4 (i, −1, −i, 1), so iⁿ depends only on n mod 4.

    Sequences and series. Arithmetic progression: nth term a + (n−1)d; sum S = n/2·[2a + (n−1)d] = n/2·(first + last). Geometric progression: nth term arⁿ⁻¹; sum S = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); infinite sum S∞ = a/(1 − r) valid only when |r| < 1. Trap: "sum to infinity" questions always need the |r| < 1 check; 1 + 2 + 4 + … has no finite infinite sum.

    Logarithms. log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log(aⁿ) = n·log a; log_b a = (log a)/(log b); b^(log_b x) = x. Domain trap: log x exists only for x > 0, and the base must be positive and ≠ 1 — equations like log_x 8 = 3 demand you check the base afterwards.

    Matrices and determinants. A 2×2 inverse: 1/(ad − bc)·[[d, −b],[−c, a]] — swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant. |AB| = |A|·|B|; |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|; |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹ for an n×n matrix. A square matrix is invertible only if |A| ≠ 0 (singular otherwise). Trap: matrix multiplication is not commutative (AB ≠ BA in general) and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ, not AᵀBᵀ.

    Trigonometry

    Core identities. ; ; . Compound angles: ; ; . Double angles: ; ; .

    Standard values (memorise cold): ; cos runs the same list backwards; tan 0°/30°/45°/60° = 0, 1/√3, 1, √3 (tan 90° undefined). Degree–radian conversion: . Trap: calculators and NDA questions default to radians in calculus contexts — a "sin x" inside a derivative is in radians.

    Triangle solutions. Sine rule: (R = circumradius). Cosine rule: . (Heron, s = semiperimeter). Heights and distances: angle of elevation/depression problems are just right-triangle tan ratios — draw the diagram first, label the known angle at the observer's eye, and check whether the question wants the height above ground or above the observer.

    Differential and integral calculus

    Standard limits. ; ; ; . The 0/0 form is the signal to apply these or L'Hôpital's rule.

    Differentiation. ; sin→cos; cos→−sin; tan→sec²x; eˣ→eˣ; ln x→1/x; aˣ→aˣ·ln a. Product rule: . Quotient rule: . Chain rule: — the most-tested rule in NDA calculus. Second derivative f″ decides concavity; at a stationary point (f′ = 0), f″ > 0 means a minimum and f″ < 0 means a maximum. |x| is not differentiable at x = 0 (sharp corner) — a classic trap.

    Integration. (n ≠ −1); ; ; ; ; . Definite integral ; area under a curve is the definite integral of (upper − lower) between intersection points. Differential equations: order = highest derivative present; degree = power of the highest derivative after clearing radicals — find order first, then degree.

    Statistics and probability

    Central tendency and dispersion. Mean x̄ = Σx/n; median = middle value of ordered data (average of the two middle values for even n); mode = most frequent value. Variance σ² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (population) — note NDA usually uses n, not n−1; standard deviation = √variance; coefficient of variation = σ/x̄. Trap: variance of a constant dataset is 0, and adding a constant to all data shifts the mean but leaves variance unchanged, while multiplying all data by k multiplies the SD by |k| and the variance by k².

    Probability. P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes. Addition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) (drop the last term only if mutually exclusive). Multiplication: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Complement: P(not E) = 1 − P(E). Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Binomial: P(X = k) = C(n,k)·pᵏ·qⁿ⁻ᵏ, mean = np, variance = npq. Trap: "at least one" questions are fastest via the complement; and two events being mutually exclusive does not make them independent (except trivial cases) — examiners love blurring this.

    2. English Grammar & Vocabulary

    English is 50 questions in the NDA GAT, a full 120-question paper in CDS, and the section where AFCAT and Agniveer candidates bleed the most avoidable marks. Expect spotting errors, sentence improvement, synonyms/antonyms, idioms, sentence ordering, comprehension and cloze tests. Grammar is rule-based — learn a rule once, use it forever; vocabulary is won through word-families.

    Subject–verb agreement

    The verb agrees with the subject, never with a phrase parked between them: "The box of chocolates was on the table" (subject = box). Either/or and neither/nor take the number of the nearer subject: "Neither the soldiers nor the officer was informed." Each, every, either, neither, one, anyone, nobody take singular verbs: "Each of the cadets has a rifle." "One of the + plural noun" takes a singular verb: "One of the pilots is injured." "The number of recruits is rising" (singular) but "A number of recruits are waiting" (plural). "Many a soldier has fallen" — many a is singular. Trap: "The quality of the apples was good" — of-phrases never change the verb's number.

    Tenses

    Twelve forms, four families. Simple: "He drills daily / drilled yesterday / will drill tomorrow." Continuous: "is drilling / was drilling / will be drilling." Perfect: "has drilled / had drilled / will have drilled." Perfect continuous: "has been drilling since 2020." High-yield rules: since + point of time and for + duration pair with perfect tenses ("I have served since 2019", "for three years"). With "by the time", use past perfect in the earlier clause: "By the time the parade started, the chief guest had arrived." After "no sooner", use "than" (not "but"): "No sooner had he fired than the target fell." Trap: "I am living here since 2020" is wrong — since/for forces "have been living". Conditionals: Type 1 (If it rains, we will cancel), Type 2 (If I were you, I would apply), Type 3 (If he had trained, he would have passed). "Were" after if/as if is subjunctive — "I wish I were taller" is correct.

    Articles and prepositions

    "A" before consonant sounds, "an" before vowel sounds — sound, not letter: "an hour", "a university", "an honest officer". "The" for unique things (the sun), superlatives (the bravest), rivers/seas/mountain ranges (the Ganga, the Himalayas), and previously mentioned nouns. Memorise these preposition pairings — they appear every year: afraid of, good at, depend on/upon, interested in, married to, different from, deal with (a person) / deal in (goods), consist of, accused of, capable of, according to, in spite of, senior/junior/superior/inferior to (never "than"), prefer to (not "than"), congratulate on, insist on, arrive at (a place) / arrive in (a country or city).

    Voice and narration

    Active↔passive follows tense-wise formulas: Simple present "She writes reports" → "Reports are written by her"; past "wrote" → "were written"; future "will write" → "will be written"; continuous "is writing" → "is being written"; perfect "has written" → "has been written". In narration, backshift one step: present→past, past→past perfect, will→would, can→could; "this"→"that", "here"→"there", "today"→"that day". Universal truths and habitual facts do not backshift: He said, "The sun rises in the east" → He said that the sun rises in the east. Questions become "asked + if/whether" or the wh-word; imperatives become "ordered/requested/advised + to-infinitive". Trap: "said to me" becomes "told me" — "told to me" is wrong.

    Vocabulary through word-families

    Learn roots and one root unlocks dozens of words: dict (say) — predict, dictate, verdict, indict; graph/gram (write) — biography, telegram, grammar; phon (sound) — telephone, symphony, cacophony; chron (time) — chronic, chronicle, anachronism; therm (heat) — thermal, thermometer; port (carry) — import, portable, deport; scrib/script (write) — describe, manuscript, prescribe; bene (good) — benefit, benevolent; mal (bad) — malice, malfunction; anthro (human) — anthropology, misanthrope. Prefixes flip or shade meaning: un-/in-/im-/dis-/mis-/anti-/pre-/re-. For synonyms/antonyms, NDA recycles a core set: candid (frank) ↔ evasive; diligent ↔ indolent; frugal ↔ extravagant; lucid ↔ obscure; transient ↔ permanent; novice ↔ veteran; ascent ↔ descent; benevolent ↔ malevolent; obscure ↔ prominent; rigid ↔ flexible.

    Idioms and phrasal verbs (high-frequency in papers): to bite the dust (be defeated); to burn the midnight oil (study late); a blessing in disguise; to call a spade a spade (speak plainly); once in a blue moon; to beat around the bush; to break the ice; to face the music; to let the cat out of the bag; a wild goose chase; to spill the beans; under the weather (ill); to hit the nail on the head; to throw in the towel (give up); at sixes and sevens (confused). Phrasal verbs: bring up (raise/mention), call off (cancel), look into (investigate), put off (postpone), run into (meet by chance), set up (establish), take over (assume control), turn down (reject), break down (fail/collapse), carry out (execute), give up (quit), look after (care for), put up with (tolerate).

    One-word substitutions: one who can use both hands — ambidextrous; fear of heights — acrophobia; government by the rich — plutocracy; murder of a king — regicide; of one's brother — fratricide; a remedy for all diseases — panacea; one who lives on others — parasite. Confusables: affect (influence, verb) / effect (result, noun); accept / except; advice (noun) / advise (verb); complement (complete) / compliment (praise); principal (head/chief) / principle (rule); stationary (still) / stationery (paper); their / there / they're; lose / loose; desert (abandon/arid land) / dessert (sweet).

    Comprehension and cloze strategy

    Read the questions before the passage so you know what to hunt. Answer only from the passage — never from outside knowledge or opinion. In cloze tests, read the whole paragraph first, fill easy blanks, then use collocations (words that travel together: "take advantage of", "pay attention to") and grammar signals (a/an/the, tense consistency) for the rest. In sentence ordering, find the opening sentence (usually a general statement, never starting with "however/therefore/they"), then chain pronoun references — "he/they/this" must point backwards to an already-introduced noun.

    3. Physics

    Physics is the largest science block in the NDA GAT and a steady 8–12 questions in Agniveer and CDS GK. Questions are concept-first: units, sign conventions and vector-vs-scalar distinctions decide more marks than memorised derivations.

    Units, dimensions and motion

    SI base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount), candela (luminous intensity). Derived units to know by heart: newton (kg·m/s²), joule (N·m), watt (J/s), pascal (N/m²), volt (J/C), ohm, tesla, hertz. Kinematics at constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as. Vectors (displacement, velocity, force, momentum) have direction; scalars (distance, speed, work, energy, temperature) do not — distance can exceed displacement but never be less. Projectile range R = u²sin2θ/g is maximum at 45°; time of flight = 2u·sinθ/g.

    Newton's laws, friction and circular motion

    First law: inertia — bodies resist changes to rest or uniform motion; this is why seatbelts matter. Second: F = ma; equivalently, force equals rate of change of momentum (F = dp/dt). Third: action–reaction pairs act on different bodies, so they never cancel — the classic trap. Weight = mg; mass is invariant, weight changes with g (about one-sixth on the Moon). Friction opposes relative motion: static friction ≤ μₛN adjusts up to its limit; kinetic friction = μₖN is roughly constant and usually less than maximum static — which is why it is harder to start pushing a crate than to keep it sliding. Centripetal force mv²/r points to the centre; the "centrifugal force" you feel in a turning vehicle is a pseudo-force in the rotating frame — examiners ask this directly.

    Work, energy, power and momentum

    Work W = F·s·cosθ — zero when force is perpendicular to displacement (a porter carrying luggage horizontally does no work against gravity; uniform circular motion does no work). Kinetic energy ½mv²; potential mgh (gravitational) and ½kx² (spring). Power P = W/t = F·v. Conservation of mechanical energy: in the absence of non-conservative forces, KE + PE is constant — falling bodies trade height for speed. Momentum p = mv is conserved in collisions when no external impulse acts; impulse J = F·Δt = Δp. Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy too; inelastic ones convert some to heat/sound. Escape velocity from Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s; orbital velocity of a low satellite ≈ 7.9 km/s.

    Gravitation, fluids and heat

    Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r²; g = GM/R² decreases with altitude and depth, and is maximum at the surface. Pressure P = F/A; atmospheric pressure ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (1 atm = 760 mm Hg) measured by barometer. Pascal's law (pressure transmits undiminished) drives hydraulic lifts and brakes. Archimedes' principle: buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid — ships float because their average density (hull + air) is below water's; a steel block sinks but a steel ship floats. Bernoulli's principle (faster fluid, lower pressure) explains aerofoil lift, the Bunsen burner and why roofs blow off in storms. Heat: conduction (solids, metals best), convection (fluids), radiation (no medium needed — the Sun's heat reaches us this way). Anomalous expansion: water is densest at 4°C — lakes freeze top-down, preserving aquatic life.

    Waves, sound and light

    Wave speed v = fλ. Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave: needs a medium, fastest in solids, slowest in gases (~343 m/s in air at 20°C), and cannot travel in vacuum. Audible range 20 Hz–20 kHz; infrasonic < 20 Hz (elephants, earthquakes), ultrasonic > 20 kHz (bats, SONAR, medical imaging). Echo ranging: distance = (speed × time)/2 — divide by two because the sound travels there and back; this is the standard trap. Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave (~3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum). Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection; plane mirrors give virtual, erect, same-size images with left-right reversal. Refraction follows Snell's law n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂; total internal reflection (denser→rarer, beyond the critical angle) creates mirages, sparkling diamonds and optical-fibre guiding. Lenses: convex converges (used for hypermetropia/farsightedness), concave diverges (myopia/nearsightedness); lens formula 1/f = 1/v − 1/u with Cartesian sign conventions. Dispersion through a prism: violet deviates most, red least (VIBGYOR order) — rainbows are dispersion + total internal reflection in droplets. The sky is blue from Rayleigh scattering (short wavelengths scatter most); sunrises/sunsets are red because blue is scattered away over the long path.

    Electricity, magnetism and modern physics

    Current I = Q/t (ampere). Ohm's law V = IR; resistance R = ρL/A — longer/thinner wires resist more. Series: same current, voltages add, R_eq = R₁ + R₂; parallel: same voltage, currents add, 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ — household wiring is parallel so each appliance gets full voltage. Electric power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; domestic energy is billed in kilowatt-hours (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 1 unit). Magnetism: like poles repel; a current-carrying wire circles itself with magnetic field (right-hand thumb rule); Fleming's left-hand rule gives motor force direction, the right-hand rule gives generator/dynamo induced current. Electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law) — changing flux induces EMF — is the principle of transformers, generators and induction stoves; transformers work only on AC. Modern physics: the photoelectric effect (Einstein) proves light's particle nature — emission depends on frequency, not intensity. Nuclear: fission (heavy nucleus splits — reactors, atom bomb) vs fusion (light nuclei merge — Sun, hydrogen bomb); moderators (heavy water, graphite) slow neutrons; control rods (cadmium, boron) absorb them. Radioactivity: α (helium nucleus, stopped by paper), β (electron, stopped by aluminium), γ (EM wave, needs lead); half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay.

    Common traps. (1) Speed vs velocity in formulas — momentum and KE need the vector/scalar distinction. (2) g = 0 does not mean weightlessness needs zero gravity — orbiting astronauts are in free fall. (3) "Which colour deviates most in a prism?" — violet, not red. (4) Fuse wire goes in series with the live wire, of low melting point and high resistance. (5) A transformer cannot work on DC.

    4. Chemistry

    Chemistry in defence exams is the most scoring science subject because it is almost entirely factual and Class X–XII NCERT-based: atomic structure, the periodic table, acids–bases–salts, metals and non-metals, carbon compounds and everyday chemistry cover roughly 80% of questions. Learn the trends and the named substances below and chemistry becomes free marks.

    Atomic structure

    Atom = protons + neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells. Proton (positive, mass ≈ 1 u, discovered via canal rays/Goldstein), neutron (neutral, ≈ 1 u, Chadwick 1932), electron (negative, negligible mass, J.J. Thomson). Atomic number Z = number of protons (defines the element); mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes: same Z, different A (protium ¹H, deuterium ²H, tritium ³H; C-12/C-14 used in radiocarbon dating; U-235/U-238). Bohr's model: electrons revolve in fixed orbits with quantised angular momentum; energy is absorbed/emitted only in jumps between shells (n = 1 K, 2 L, 3 M, 4 N). Maximum electrons in shell n = 2n² (2, 8, 18, 32). Electronic configuration follows Aufbau order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p… — note 4s fills before 3d (K: 2,8,8,1; Ca: 2,8,8,2). Quantum numbers: principal n (shell/size), azimuthal l (subshell shape: s, p, d, f), magnetic m (orientation), spin s (±½). Valency = combining capacity, determined by outermost-shell electrons; noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have full outer shells and are inert — Group 18.

    The periodic table and bonding

    Modern periodic law (Moseley): properties are periodic functions of atomic number. Periods (7 horizontal rows) = number of shells; groups (18 vertical columns) = valence electrons. Trends across a period (left→right): atomic size decreases, ionisation energy and electronegativity increase, metallic character decreases. Down a group: size increases, ionisation energy decreases, metallic character increases. Most electronegative element: fluorine; most electropositive stable metal: francium (practically, caesium). Lanthanides and actinides are the inner transition (f-block) series.

    Chemical bonding. Ionic (electrovalent): transfer of electrons — NaCl, MgO; high melting points, conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, brittle. Covalent: sharing — H₂, Cl₂, CH₄, diamond; generally low melting points, poor conductors. Coordinate (dative): one atom donates both electrons — NH₄⁺, CO. Hydrogen bonding (H attached to F/O/N attracted to another F/O/N) explains water's high boiling point and ice floating. Metallic bonding: sea of delocalised electrons — conductivity, malleability, ductility, lustre. Trap: diamond and graphite are both pure carbon — diamond is the hardest natural substance (3D covalent network), graphite conducts electricity and is used in pencils and as a lubricant (layered structure with delocalised electrons).

    Mole concept, acids, bases and salts

    One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number); at STP one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L. Molar mass links grams to moles: n = mass/molar mass. Acids (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, CH₃COOH) release H⁺ in water, turn blue litmus red, taste sour; bases (NaOH, Ca(OH)₂, NH₄OH) release OH⁻, turn red litmus blue, feel soapy. pH scale 0–14: < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic; each unit is a 10× change in H⁺ concentration. Human blood pH ≈ 7.4; stomach HCl ≈ pH 1–2; acid rain < 5.6. Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. Important salts: common salt NaCl; washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; baking soda NaHCO₃ (antacid, fire extinguishers, baking); plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O (sets with water to gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O — used for casts and statues); bleaching powder CaOCl₂ (disinfectant); lime: quicklime CaO + water → slaked lime Ca(OH)₂ (whitewashing).

    Metals, non-metals and extraction

    Reactivity series (memorise): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt. Metals above hydrogen displace it from acids; a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt (iron displaces copper from CuSO₄ — the blue solution turns green). Extraction: highly reactive metals (Na, Ca, Al) by electrolysis; moderately reactive (Zn, Fe, Pb) by reduction of oxides with carbon/coke (smelting); least reactive (Ag, Au, Pt) found native or by simple heating. Iron: haematite (Fe₂O₃) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄) ores, extracted in the blast furnace; cast iron (2–4% C, brittle), wrought iron (purest, <0.1% C), steel (controlled carbon + alloying). Stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni (corrosion-resistant). Corrosion of iron = rusting (needs both air and moisture); prevented by painting, oiling, galvanisation (zinc coating — zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes first: sacrificial protection), and alloying. Copper + tin = bronze; copper + zinc = brass; lead + tin = solder; aluminium + copper = duralumin (aircraft). Mercury is the only liquid metal; bromine the only liquid non-metal; tungsten has the highest melting point (bulb filaments); silver is the best electrical conductor, copper the practical choice.

    Carbon compounds and everyday chemistry

    Carbon's tetravalency and catenation (self-linking) create organic chemistry. Hydrocarbons: alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (methane CH₄ — natural gas/biogas main component), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (ethene), alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne/acetylene — welding). Functional groups: –OH alcohol (ethanol — liquor, sanitiser), –COOH carboxylic acid (acetic acid — vinegar), –CHO aldehyde, ketone (acetone — nail-polish remover). LPG = butane + propane (odourless; ethyl mercaptan added for leak detection); CNG = mainly methane; biogas = methane + CO₂; water gas = CO + H₂; producer gas = CO + N₂. Cement = limestone + clay heated (clinker) + gypsum; glass = silica + sodium carbonate + limestone (coloured by metal oxides — cobalt blue, chromium green); fertilisers: urea (46% N, highest nitrogen), NPK complexes; baking powder = baking soda + tartaric acid. Air pollution: CO (from incomplete combustion — binds haemoglobin), SO₂/NOₓ (acid rain), CFCs (ozone depletion — Montreal Protocol).

    Common traps. (1) Dry HCl gas does not turn litmus — acids show acidic behaviour only in aqueous solution. (2) Diamond conducts heat but not electricity; graphite conducts electricity. (3) pH is logarithmic — pH 3 is 100× more acidic than pH 5, not "2 more". (4) "Laughing gas" is nitrous oxide N₂O; "tear gas" is chloropicrin/CN gas — know the nicknames. (5) Aqua regia (3:1 HCl:HNO₃) dissolves gold and platinum — neither acid alone can.

    5. Biology

    Biology is the "general science" backbone of the NDA GAT and a fixed 6–10 questions in Agniveer papers. The syllabus is Class X NCERT plus human physiology: the cell, plant processes, human body systems, nutrition, diseases and ecology. Questions are direct — name the organelle, the vitamin, the vector — so breadth with precise one-line facts beats deep theory.

    The cell and plant physiology

    Robert Hooke coined "cell" (1665); Robert Brown discovered the nucleus. The cell is the structural and functional unit of life. Organelles: nucleus (control centre, contains chromosomes/DNA); mitochondria (powerhouse — cellular respiration, ATP); chloroplasts (photosynthesis — only in plants); ribosomes (protein synthesis); endoplasmic reticulum (transport; rough has ribosomes); Golgi bodies (packaging/secretion); lysosomes (suicide bags — digestion, autolysis); vacuoles (storage; large in plant cells); cell wall (cellulose — plants only, gives rigidity); cell membrane (selectively permeable — all cells).

    Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O →(light/chlorophyll) C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — in leaves, chlorophyll traps light, stomata admit CO₂, xylem supplies water. Transpiration pulls the transpiration stream upward; respiration C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy runs in all living cells, day and night. Aerobic respiration (with O₂) yields far more energy than anaerobic (yeast: alcoholic fermentation; muscles: lactic acid). Plant hormones: auxins (growth, phototropism), gibberellins (stem growth), cytokinins (cell division), abscisic acid (dormancy), ethylene (fruit ripening).

    Human body systems

    Digestive system: mouth (salivary amylase starts starch digestion) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (HCl + pepsin digest protein; mucus protects the wall) → small intestine (complete digestion and absorption via villi; receives bile from the liver — emulsifies fats — and pancreatic juice with amylase, trypsin, lipase) → large intestine (water absorption) → rectum. Liver is the largest gland: secretes bile, stores glycogen, detoxifies, makes urea.

    Respiratory system: nostrils → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea (rings of cartilage) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (gas exchange; huge surface area, rich capillaries). Haemoglobin in RBCs carries O₂ (oxyhaemoglobin — bright red) and some CO₂; CO poisoning works because CO binds haemoglobin ~200× more strongly than O₂.

    Circulatory system: the heart is a four-chambered double pump — right side handles deoxygenated blood (body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs), left side oxygenated (lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body). Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, elastic walls; mostly oxygenated — the pulmonary artery is the exception), veins return it (valves; mostly deoxygenated — the pulmonary vein is the exception), capillaries exchange materials. Blood: RBCs (no nucleus in mammals, carry O₂, lifespan ~120 days, made in bone marrow), WBCs (immunity — phagocytosis; raised count signals infection), platelets (clotting). Blood groups ABO + Rh: O is the universal donor (no antigens), AB the universal recipient (no antibodies).

    Excretion and control: kidneys filter blood — nephron is the functional unit. Nervous system: brain (cerebrum — thought/memory; cerebellum — balance/coordination; medulla — involuntary actions: breathing, heartbeat, BP) → spinal cord → nerves; reflex arc bypasses the brain for speed (knee jerk). Endocrine glands (ductless, hormones into blood): pituitary (master gland — growth hormone; excess in childhood → gigantism, deficiency → dwarfism), thyroid (thyroxine — needs iodine; deficiency → goitre, cretinism), parathyroid (calcium), adrenal (adrenaline — fight-or-flight, at the kidney tops), pancreas (insulin + glucagon — diabetes is insulin deficiency/excess sugar), testes (testosterone), ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone).

    Nutrition, disease and genetics

    Vitamins and deficiency diseases (memorise as a table): A (retinol — night blindness, xerophthalmia); B1 (thiamine — beriberi); B2 (riboflavin — cheilosis); B3 (niacin — pellagra); B9 (folic acid — neural tube defects, anaemia); B12 (cyanocobalamin — pernicious anaemia; only vitamin with cobalt; only one not reliably available from plants); C (ascorbic acid — scurvy; richest sources: amla, guava, citrus); D (calciferol — rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults; synthesised in skin by sunlight); E (tocopherol — antioxidant, fertility vitamin); K (phylloquinone — clotting; made by gut bacteria). Minerals: iron (haemoglobin — anaemia), iodine (thyroxine — goitre), calcium + phosphorus (bones/teeth), zinc (immunity), fluorine excess (fluorosis).

    Diseases: Bacterial — TB (Mycobacterium tuberculosis; BCG vaccine; DOTS treatment), cholera (Vibrio — ORS is the lifesaver), typhoid (Salmonella typhi — Widal test), tetanus (lockjaw; Clostridium). Viral — common cold, influenza, dengue/chikungunya (Aedes mosquito), malaria is protozoan (Plasmodium, Anopheles vector), AIDS (HIV — retrovirus; ELISA test), rabies (dog bite), hepatitis (A/E water-borne; B/C blood-borne), polio (oral OPV — pulse polio), COVID-19 (coronavirus). Fungal — ringworm, athlete's foot. Non-communicable — diabetes, hypertension, cancer (uncontrolled cell division; carcinogens; biopsy diagnosis), coronary disease. Vaccines: BCG (TB), DPT (diphtheria/pertussis/tetanus), OPV (polio), MMR (measles/mumps/rubella). Vectors: mosquito — malaria/dengue/chikungunya/filariasis; housefly — cholera/typhoid (mechanical); tsetse fly — sleeping sickness; sandfly — kala-azar.

    Genetics basics: Mendel's laws (dominance, segregation, independent assortment) from pea plants. DNA double helix (Watson & Crick, 1953, on Franklin's data): A–T, G–C base pairing; genes are DNA segments; chromosomes carry them (humans: 46 = 23 pairs; 23rd pair XX/XY decides sex — the Y chromosome from the father determines maleness). Blood groups and haemophilia/colour blindness are classic inheritance questions — haemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked recessive, so males show them more often.

    Ecology in one page

    Ecosystem = biotic community + abiotic environment. Producers (green plants) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary (small carnivores) → tertiary (top carnivores); decomposers (bacteria, fungi) recycle everything. Only ~10% of energy transfers between trophic levels (Lindeman's 10% law) — hence food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels and biomass pyramids narrow upward. Symbiosis: mutualism (lichen = algae + fungi; Rhizobium + legumes), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected), parasitism (one harmed). Biosphere reserves, national parks (no human activity) vs sanctuaries (limited activity) vs biosphere reserves (zoned) — asked as differences. Ozone layer (stratosphere) blocks UV; greenhouse gases CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, CFCs drive warming.

    Common traps. (1) Malaria is protozoan, not viral/bacterial. (2) The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — "artery = oxygenated" fails here. (3) Reflex actions are controlled by the spinal cord, not the brain. (4) Insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it — diabetes questions hinge on this pair. (5) Xylem carries water up, phloem carries food both ways.

    6. History: Ancient, Medieval & Modern India

    History is the heaviest GS block in the NDA GAT and CDS GK — typically 15–25 questions — and it rewards chronological thinking over rote dates.

    Ancient India

    Indus Valley Civilisation (~2600–1900 BCE): first discovered site Harappa (1921, R.D. Banerji/Dayaram Sahni excavations), most famous Mohenjo-daro ("mound of the dead", Great Bath, Great Granary, bronze Dancing Girl). Town planning: grid streets, covered drains, citadel + lower town; standardised weights; seals (steatite, unicorn motif — script undeciphered). Other key sites: Lothal (dockyard — Gujarat), Kalibangan (ploughed field, fire altars), Rakhigarhi (largest Indian site, Haryana).

    Vedic period: Early Vedic (~1500–1000 BCE) — Rigveda (oldest text; 10 mandalas; Gayatri mantra in Mandala 3), society of janas under a rajan. Later Vedic (~1000–600 BCE) — Sama/Yajur/Atharva Vedas (Brahmanas, Upanishads — "Satyameva Jayate" from the Mundaka Upanishad). Mahajanapadas (6th century BCE): 16 kingdoms — Magadha (strongest; Bimbisara, Ajatashatru), Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti prominent; capitals Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Ujjain. This century also produced Mahavira (Jainism — 24th Tirthankara; ahimsa central) and Buddha (born Lumbini 563 BCE; enlightenment Bodh Gaya; first sermon Sarnath — Dharmachakra; mahaparinirvana Kushinagar; Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path; councils at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra, Kashmir).

    Mauryan Empire (321–185 BCE): founded by Chandragupta Maurya (guided by Chanakya's Arthashastra); Bindusara; Ashoka (273–232 BCE) — Kalinga war (261 BCE) converted him to Dhamma; edicts in Prakrit/Brahmi script (James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi) on rocks and pillars; lion capital of Sarnath is India's national emblem. Post-Mauryan: Kanishka (78 CE; Saka era begins; 4th Buddhist council in Kashmir; Gandhara art flourishes). Gupta Age (320–550 CE) — "Golden Age": Chandragupta I, Samudragupta (Allahabad pillar prashasti by Harisena — "Napoleon of India"), Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (Fa-Hien visited; Aryabhata's astronomy — place value, zero, π approximation), Kumaragupta (founded Nalanda university). Art: Ajanta cave paintings, Sarnath Buddha, Dashavatara temple. Harsha (606–647 CE): capital Kannauj; defeated by Pulakeshin II (Chalukya) at the Narmada.

    Medieval India

    Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) — five dynasties in order: Slave/Mamluk (Qutb-ud-din Aibak — Qutub Minar begun; Iltutmish — completed Qutub Minar; Razia Sultan — first woman ruler; Balban — theory of kingship, "Divine Right"), Khalji (Alauddin Khalji — market reforms/price control), Tughlaq (Ghiyasuddin; Muhammad bin Tughlaq — token currency, capital shift to Daulatabad, both failed), Sayyid, Lodi (Bahlol; Sikandar — founded Agra 1504; Ibrahim Lodi — defeated by Babur at Panipat 1526). Vijayanagara (1336–1646): founded by Harihara and Bukka; Krishnadevaraya (1509–29, Tuluva dynasty — golden age); Battle of Talikota 1565 (alliance of Deccan sultanates destroyed the city). Bhakti & Sufi: Bhakti saints — Ramananda, Kabir (dohas, nirguna), Guru Nanak (1469–1539); Sufi orders — Chishti (Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, Ajmer) most popular.

    Mughals (1526–1857 titular): Babur (Panipat 1526 — first use of gunpowder/artillery in North India; Tuzuk-i-Baburi); Humayun (lost to Sher Shah Suri at Chausa 1539/Kannauj 1540 — Sher Shah's reforms: rupiya currency, Grand Trunk Road, land revenue zabt; Humayun regained 1555); Akbar (1556–1605 — regent Bairam Khan; Panipat II 1556 vs Hemu; mansabdari system, zabt revenue under Todar Mal, Din-i-Ilahi 1582; Navratnas incl. Birbal, Tansen, Abul Fazl — Ain-i-Akbari/Akbarnama); Jahangir (chain of justice; Nur Jahan's influence; English factory at Surat 1613); Shah Jahan (1638–58 — Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Peacock Throne; golden age of architecture); Aurangzeb (1658–1707 — Deccan obsession, jizya reimposed, executed Guru Tegh Bahadur 1675, wars with Marathas/Sikhs/Jats; empire reached maximum extent, seeds of decline). Marathas: Shivaji (1627–80 — coronation 1674 at Raigad; Ashtapradhan council); Peshwas — Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I; Third Battle of Panipat 1761 (Ahmad Shah Abdali's victory opened the door to British supremacy). Sikh Gurus in sequence: Nanak → Angad → Amar Das → Ram Das → Arjan → Hargobind → Har Rai → Harkrishan → Tegh Bahadur → Gobind Singh (Khalsa 1699).

    Modern India

    British consolidation: Battle of Plassey 1757 (Clive vs Siraj-ud-daulah — betrayal by Mir Jafar), Buxar 1764 (Hector Munro vs combined Mir Qasim/Shuja-ud-daula/Shah Alam II — the real foundation of British power; Treaty of Allahabad 1765 gave Diwani of Bengal). Regulating Act 1773 (Warren Hastings — first Governor-General), Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Acts 1833 (Governor-General of India — Bentinck; Macaulay's education minute 1835; English official language), Revolt of 1857 (Meerut 10 May; leaders: Rani Lakshmibai — Jhansi, Nana Sahib — Kanpur, Tantia Tope, Begum Hazrat Mahal — Lucknow, Kunwar Singh — Bihar; causes: greased cartridges, Doctrine of Lapse, annexations; failed from lack of unity and leadership ). Government of India Act 1858 (Crown rule; Canning — first Viceroy).

    National movement: INC founded 1885 (A.O. Hume; first session Bombay, W.C. Bonnerjee president). Partition of Bengal 1905 (Curzon) → Swadeshi movement; annulled 1911 (Delhi Durbar — capital shifted Calcutta→Delhi). Morley-Minto 1909 (separate electorates — "divide and rule" seed); Lucknow Pact 1916 (Congress–League unity; Tilak and Jinnah); Montagu-Chelmsford 1919 (dyarchy). Gandhi era: returned 1915; Champaran 1917 (indigo), Kheda 1918, Ahmedabad mill strike 1918; Rowlatt Act 1919 → Jallianwala Bagh 13 April 1919 (Dyer; Hunter Committee); Non-Cooperation 1920–22 (withdrawn after Chauri Chaura); Simon Commission 1927 (boycott — "Simon go back"); Lahore session Dec 1929 (Purna Swaraj; 26 Jan celebrated as Independence Day); Civil Disobedience 1930 — Dandi March 12 March 1930 (Sabarmati→Dandi; salt law broken); Round Table Conferences (Gandhi attended only the second); Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, federal scheme); Quit India 8 August 1942 ("Do or Die"; Gandhi, Nehru, Patel jailed); INA — Subhas Chandra Bose (Azad Hind Fauj 1943); Cabinet Mission 1946; Indian Independence Act July 1947; 15 August 1947 — midnight "Tryst with Destiny" (Nehru); Radcliffe Line; Patel integrated 562 princely states (Hyderabad by police action 1948, Junagadh plebiscite, Kashmir — Instrument of Accession 26 Oct 1947).

    Revolutionary strand: Ghadar Party 1913 (Har Dayal), Kakori 1925 (Bismil, Ashfaqulla hanged), HSRA — Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru (hanged 23 March 1931), Chittagong armoury raid 1930 (Surya Sen).

    Common traps. (1) Saka era (78 CE) = Kanishka, not Vikramaditya — Vikram Samvat is 57 BCE. (2) The national emblem's lions are Ashokan (Sarnath); the motto "Satyameva Jayate" is from the Mundaka Upanishad. (3) Firsts: first Governor-General of independent India — Mountbatten; first Indian Governor-General — C. Rajagopalachari; first President — Rajendra Prasad. (4) Jallianwala Bagh (1919) preceded Non-Cooperation (1920) — sequence questions love this.

    7. Geography: Terrain, Borders & Strategic Geography

    Defence exams love geography because a soldier's world is a map. Roughly a third of NDA GAT geography questions — and a large slice of CDS/AFCAT general-awareness questions — come from terrain, borders, strategic locations, and India's neighbourhood. Master the places in this chapter and you can also decode questions about exercises, deployments, and conflict zones.

    India's land borders: the three frontiers

    Western frontier (Pakistan, ~3,323 km): From Gujarat's Rann of Kutch to J&K, the border comprises the international boundary, the Line of Control (LoC, ~740 km) in J&K, and the Actual Ground Position Line (AGPL, ~110 km) across the Siachen Glacier. Key exam facts: the LoC originated from the 1972 Shimla Agreement (it replaced the 1949 CFL), and Siachen — the world's highest battlefield — was occupied by India in Operation Meghdoot (April 1984), establishing the AGPL.

    Northern frontier (China, ~3,488 km): Called the Line of Actual Control (LAC), divided into Western (Ladakh, includes Aksai Chin — occupied by China), Middle (Himachal/Uttarakhand), and Eastern (Arunachal Pradesh, which China calls "South Tibet") sectors. The McMahon Line (1914) forms the basis of the eastern boundary. Ladakh was made a Union Territory in 2019 after Article 370's abrogation.

    Northeastern & eastern frontier: Nepal (~1,751 km, open border under the 1950 treaty), Bhutan (~699 km), Myanmar (~1,643 km), Bangladesh (~4,096 km — India's longest land border), and the disputed Afghanistan border in POK (~106 km).

    Strategic mountain passes and corridors

    Nathu La & Shipki La — trade passes with China (Sikkim, Himachal). Zoji La — links Kashmir valley to Ladakh (Kargil sector). Khardung La — gateway to Siachen and Nubra. Banihal Pass / Pir Panjal tunnel — Kashmir's road lifeline. Lipu Lekh — Uttarakhand tri-junction with Nepal-Tibet. Chicken's Neck (Siliguri Corridor, ~22 km wide) — connects mainland India to the Northeast, flanked by Nepal, Bhutan, and Bangladesh; the Doklam plateau (2017 standoff) sits just north of it. Tunnel projects to memorise: Atal Tunnel (Rohtang), Z-Morh and Zojila tunnels (Ladakh connectivity).

    Maritime geography and island territories

    India's 7,516 km coastline spans 9 coastal states and 4 UTs. Strategic chokepoints: Strait of Malacca (India's Andaman & Nicobar Islands sit astride its western approaches — the "unsinkable aircraft carrier"), Palk Strait, Gulf of Mannar, Strait of Hormuz (oil imports), and the Mozambique Channel. Andaman & Nicobar Command at Port Blair is India's only tri-service theatre command. Lakshadweep guards the Arabian Sea's Nine Degree Channel. Remember: INS Baaz (Campbell Bay, southernmost airbase), Indira Point (southernmost tip of India, Great Nicobar).

    World geography for defence questions

    Memorise these perennial exam favourites: Gulf of Aden / Bab-el-Mandeb (anti-piracy patrols), South China Sea (disputed: China's nine-dash line vs Philippines/Vietnam claims; India runs oil exploration with Vietnam), Diego Garcia (US base in the Indian Ocean, Chagos Islands), Djibouti (China's first overseas military base), Gwadar (Pakistan, CPEC terminus) vs Chabahar (Iran, India's gateway to Central Asia), Hambantota (Sri Lanka, Chinese-leased port). The QUAD (India-US-Japan-Australia) and Malabar exercise are the Indo-Pacific's headline security architecture.

    Rivers, monsoons and operational terrain

    The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) governs the six Indus-system rivers; India received the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) and Pakistan the western (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) — frequently in the news and exams. Terrain types drive force structure: mountain divisions for the LAC/LoC, desert warfare in the Thar (Mahajan ranges — site of Yudh Abhyas 2026's first phase), jungle warfare school at Vairengte (Mizoram), high-altitude warfare school at Gulmarg. The Thar, the Rann, the Northeast's jungles, and the Siachen glacier are the four classic Indian battle terrains examiners describe without naming. Named boundaries are pure MCQ gold: the Radcliffe Line (India-Pakistan), the Durand Line (Afghanistan-Pakistan, disputed), and the McMahon Line (India-China, eastern sector). For map-based questions, practise locating: Siachen, Doklam, Sir Creek (maritime boundary dispute), Pangong Tso, Depsang Plains, and the Galwan valley (June 2020 clash).

    8. Polity & Defence Economy: How the Military Is Governed and Funded

    Defence aspirants meet the Constitution twice: once in the written exam's polity section, and again at the SSB interview when the assessor asks "who commands the armed forces?" This chapter covers the constitutional framework, the Ministry of Defence's machinery, and the economics of defence — all exam staples.

    Constitutional command structure

    Article 53(2): the President of India is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces — currently Droupadi Murmu. All commissions are granted in the President's name. Defence is in the Union List (List I), so Parliament alone legislates on it. Emergency provisions matter for defence exams: a National Emergency (Article 352) has been proclaimed three times — 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war), 1975 (internal disturbance); President's Rule and Financial Emergency have never involved the military domestically. Parliament's Standing Committee on Defence examines the defence budget and CAG reports.

    The Ministry of Defence machinery

    The MoD comprises four departments: Department of Defence, Department of Military Affairs (DMA — headed by the Chief of Defence Staff, created 2019), Department of Defence Production, and Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare. The Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) — the senior-most military officer and permanent chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee — heads the DMA and advises the government on tri-service matters. Note the hierarchy examiners test: President → Government (Defence Minister) → CDS/Service Chiefs. The National Security Council (headed by the PM, advised by the NSA) handles strategic policy; the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by the Defence Minister, approves major procurements.

    Visual anchors — see the formula

    Defence budget: the big numbers

    Defence consistently receives the largest ministry allocation in the Union Budget. For FY 2026-27: ₹7,84,678 crore (~₹7.85 lakh crore), a ~15.3% jump over FY 2025-26's ₹6,81,210 crore — the first full budget after Operation Sindoor (May 2025). The structure: capital outlay ₹2,19,306 crore (~28%, for new weapons, aircraft, ships, missiles — up 21.84%), revenue expenditure ₹3,65,479 crore (salaries, operations, maintenance), and defence pensions ₹1,71,338 crore. Exam trap: pensions form part of the MoD budget but not of "defence expenditure" in some international comparisons. The capital-revenue-pension split is a favourite MCQ format.

    Atmanirbharta: the indigenisation push

    The Make in India / Atmanirbhar Bharat defence drive is now a recurring current-affairs topic. Key instruments: Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP 2020), which prioritises "Buy (Indian-IDDM)" categories; positive indigenisation lists banning imports of listed items in phases; iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) for startups; and two Defence Industrial Corridors — in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Defence production and exports have grown sharply (India now exports to 80+ countries; the often-quoted export target is ₹50,000 crore by 2029). Ordnance factories were corporatised into 7 DPSUs in 2021. Major DPSUs: HAL (aircraft), BEL (electronics/radars), BDL (missiles), MDL & GRSE (shipbuilding), DRDO (R&D, ~55 labs).

    Economy fundamentals for the defence aspirant

    NDA/CDS economics stays basic but precise: GDP vs GNP, inflation (CPI/WPI), fiscal deficit, the Union Budget process (presented 1 February), and Five-Year-Plan history (the Planning Commission became NITI Aayog in 2015). Defence economics concepts: capital vs revenue expenditure, offset clauses in defence deals, and why a rupee of defence capex multiplies through domestic industry. Also know: India's defence imports historically came mainly from Russia, now diversifying to the US, France, and Israel — a shift visible in deals like Rafale (France), Apache/Chinook and MQ-9B drones (US), and Heron/Barak systems (Israel). Finally, One Rank One Pension (OROP) — equal pension for equal rank and service length — is the landmark ex-servicemen welfare policy; it sits under the Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare and appears in both polity and current-affairs questions.

    Parliamentary and audit oversight of defence

    Defence is audited and questioned more closely than any other ministry, and examiners love the institutional names. The Standing Committee on Defence (a Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee with members from both Houses) examines the defence demands for grants, the working of the MoD, and CAG reports on procurement — its reports often surface delays like the Tejas Mk1A engine hold-up. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit defence expenditure; CAG reports on Rafale, the Kargil purchases and ammunition shortages have all become exam questions. Remember the chain: executive proposes (MoD) → Parliament votes the demands → CAG audits → PAC/Committee examines. The Defence Planning Committee (chaired by the NSA) drafts the national security strategy, while the National Security Council Secretariat supports the NSC. In war, remember the constitutional ladder tested above: the President is Supreme Commander, but operational command flows through the Defence Minister → CDS → Service Chiefs.

    How India actually buys weapons: DAP 2020 in one page

    Every big procurement follows the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020, and the stages are MCQ gold. The sequence: Services Qualitative Requirements (SQRs) → Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) by the DAC (valid for a fixed period, after which it lapses) → Request for Proposal/trials → contract. Procurement categories carry a strict preference order: Buy (Indian-IDDM) (Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured — top priority), Buy (Indian), Buy and Make (Indian), Buy (Global – Manufacture in India), and last Buy (Global). The September 2026 DAC approvals worth about ₹1.10 lakh crore, with ~98% to be sourced from Indian industry, are the textbook illustration of this hierarchy. Offsets — obligations on foreign vendors to reinvest a share of the contract value in India — and Transfer of Technology (ToT) clauses shape deals like Rafale and the MRFA programme. The positive indigenisation lists (now running into thousands of items across successive lists) ban imports of listed equipment in a phased manner, forcing domestic manufacture. The Make procedure (Make-I, II, III) funds industry-led design; the ₹586-crore Make-II contract for tank Auxiliary Power Units signed in September 2026 is a live example of Make-II in action.

    What the defence rupee does: economics of military spending

    Defence spending is the largest single-ministry outlay because it combines three budgets in one: capital (new weapons — about 28% in FY 2026-27), revenue (salaries, fuel, maintenance — the largest head), and pensions (exam trap: counted in the MoD budget but excluded from some international "military expenditure" comparisons). A rupee of domestic capital procurement multiplies through the economy: shipyards, MSMEs making components, and software for fire-control systems all sit downstream of one warship order — this is the economic logic behind the Defence Industrial Corridors in UP and Tamil Nadu and iDEX startup funding. On the external side, the goal is to flip the trade balance: India historically imported most weapons (mainly from Russia, now diversifying to the US, France and Israel), and the stated target is ₹50,000 crore in annual defence exports by 2029 — FY2025-26 already hit a record ₹38,424 crore. Know the DPSU map: HAL (aircraft), BEL (electronics/radars), BDL (missiles), MDL and GRSE (warships/submarines), MIDHANI (special metals) — plus the 7 DPSUs corporatised from the Ordnance Factory Board in 2021. OROP (One Rank One Pension) — equal pension for equal rank and length of service — is the landmark ex-servicemen welfare commitment, administered through the Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare alongside the Armed Forces Flag Day Fund and resettlement directorates. For SSB interviews, connect the economics to the mission: every indigenised system is strategic autonomy you can point to.

    9. Defence GK: Ranks, Commands, Exercises, Missiles & Wars

    This is the highest-yield chapter on the site: direct, one-mark questions that reward pure memorisation. Learn the tables cold.

    Officer ranks: the three services

    Army → Navy → Air Force: Lieutenant → Sub-Lieutenant → Flying Officer; Captain → Lieutenant → Flight Lieutenant; Major → Lieutenant Commander → Squadron Leader; Lieutenant Colonel → Commander → Wing Commander; Colonel → Captain → Group Captain; Brigadier → Commodore → Air Commodore; Major General → Rear Admiral → Air Vice Marshal; Lieutenant General → Vice Admiral → Air Marshal; General → Admiral → Air Chief Marshal. The honorary five-star ranks — Field Marshal (Sam Manekshaw, 1973; K.M. Cariappa, 1986), Admiral of the Fleet (never awarded), Marshal of the Indian Air Force (Arjan Singh, 2002) — are classic MCQs.

    Commands: Army, Navy, Air Force

    Army — 7 commands: Northern (Udhampur), Western (Chandimandir), Eastern (Kolkata), Southern (Pune), Central (Lucknow), South-Western (Jaipur), plus the training command ARTAC (Shimla). Navy — 3 commands: Western (Mumbai), Eastern (Visakhapatnam), Southern (Kochi, training). Air Force — 7 commands: Western (New Delhi), Eastern (Shillong), Central (Allahabad/Prayagraj), Southern (Thiruvananthapuram), South-Western (Gandhinagar), Maintenance (Nagpur), Training (Bengaluru). Joint: the tri-service Andaman & Nicobar Command (Port Blair) and the Strategic Forces Command (nuclear assets). Regimental centres examiners love: the Gorkha, Rajput, Sikh, Madras, and Parachute regiments, and the Rashtriya Rifles (counter-insurgency in J&K).

    Bilateral exercises by country (exam favourite)

    USA: Yudh Abhyas (Army), Malabar (Navy, now QUAD), Vajra Prahar (Special Forces), Cope India (Air Force), Tiger Triumph (tri-service). France: Shakti (Army), Varuna (Navy), Garuda (Air Force). Russia: INDRA (tri-service). UK: Ajeya Warrior (Army), Konkan (Navy), Indradhanush (Air Force). Japan: Dharma Guardian (Army), JIMEX (Navy). Australia: AUSTRAHIND (Army), AUSINDEX (Navy), Pitch Black (Air Force, multilateral). Others: Mitra Shakti (Sri Lanka), Maitree (Thailand), Garuda Shakti (Indonesia), Nomadic Elephant (Mongolia), Ekuverin (Maldives), Sampriti (Bangladesh), Khanjar (Kyrgyzstan), Surya Kiran (Nepal). Multilateral: RIMPAC (US-led naval), Bright Star (Egypt). Note for 2026: Yudh Abhyas 22 (September 2026) ran in a new two-theatre format — desert phase at Mahajan ranges (Rajasthan) plus high-altitude phase at Auli (Uttarakhand).

    Missiles and indigenous systems

    Agni series (surface-to-surface ballistic): Agni-I (700 km) to Agni-V (5,000+ km, ICBM class). Prithvi (short-range ballistic). Akash (surface-to-air). BrahMos (supersonic cruise, Indo-Russian, ~Mach 2.8–3) — the world's fastest cruise missile in its class. Nirbhay (subsonic cruise). Astra (beyond-visual-range air-to-air). Nag/Helina (anti-tank). Pinaka (multi-barrel rocket launcher). Air defence shield: Akash, MRSAM, QRSAM, VSHORADS, S-400 (Russian), plus DRDO's Kusha long-range SAM (maiden flight test July 2026). Naval assets: INS Vikrant (indigenous aircraft carrier), Arihant-class nuclear submarines (SSBN), Project-75 Scorpene submarines (Kalvari class). Aircraft: Tejas (LCA), Rafale, Su-30MKI, Apache, Chinook, C-17 Globemaster, MQ-9B Sea Guardian drones (₹1,943-crore lease).

    Wars, operations and gallantry awards

    1947-48: first Indo-Pak war over Kashmir (ceasefire 1 Jan 1949; Karachi Agreement). 1962: Sino-Indian war (Walong, Rezang La). 1965: second Indo-Pak war (Tashkent Declaration, 1966; battles of Asal Uttar, Haji Pir). 1971: Bangladesh Liberation War — India's greatest victory; 16 December is Vijay Diwas; Shimla Agreement 1972. 1984: Operation Meghdoot (Siachen). 1987-90: IPKF in Sri Lanka (Operation Pawan). 1999: Kargil War — Operation Vijay (26 July is Kargil Vijay Diwas). 2016: surgical strikes (Uri response). 2019: Balakot airstrike (Pulwama response). 2025: Operation Sindoor (May 2025) — precision strikes on terror camps in Pakistan and POJK after the Pahalgam attack; Pakistan's drone intrusions (~300–400 across 36 locations) were defeated by India's layered air defence. Gallantry hierarchy (wartime): Param Vir Chakra > Maha Vir Chakra > Vir Chakra. (Peacetime): Ashok Chakra > Kirti Chakra > Shaurya Chakra. First PVC: Major Somnath Sharma (1947, Badgam). Training academies: NDA Khadakwasla (Pune), IMA Dehradun, OTA Chennai, INA Ezhimala, AFA Dundigal (Hyderabad). Know the paramilitary distinction: CAPFs (CRPF, BSF, ITBP, SSB, CISF) fall under the Ministry of Home Affairs, not the MoD — a classic trap question. BSF guards the Pakistan/Bangladesh borders, ITBP the China border, and the Assam Rifles (under MHA operationally, officered by the Army) guards the Myanmar border.

    10. Current Affairs 2025–26: Defence & National

    Defence papers now carry 10–20 marks of recent current affairs. Below are the verified 2025–26 developments examiners are most likely to ask. Dates and figures are given as reported in Budget documents and official statements; treat any number as a snapshot that the question-setter's answer key may pin to the notification date.

    Operation Sindoor (May 2025) and its aftermath

    The defining defence event of the period. After the Pahalgam terror attack of April 2025 (26 civilians killed), India launched Operation Sindoor in May 2025 — precision strikes on terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-Occupied J&K, followed by a four-day military standoff. India destroyed terror camps, rendered several Pakistani airbases defunct, and — critically for exam questions — demonstrated its indigenous layered air defence (Akash, Pechora, OSA-AK, low-level AD guns, counter-UAS grid), which defeated roughly 300–400 Pakistani drones across 36 locations from Leh to Sir Creek. Sindoor is now the reference case for questions on drone warfare, air defence, and joint operations.

    Record defence budget FY 2026-27

    Presented 1 February 2026 by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman: ₹7,84,678 crore — India's largest-ever defence allocation, up ~15.3% from FY 2025-26's ₹6,81,210 crore, and the largest single-ministry outlay in the Union Budget. Components: capital outlay ₹2,19,306 crore (+21.84%, ~28% of the total; ₹63,733 crore for aircraft & aero engines, ₹25,023 crore for the naval fleet), revenue expenditure ₹3,65,479 crore (+17.24%), defence pensions ₹1,71,338 crore (+6.53%). The budget also cut customs duties to boost aerospace manufacturing — a favourite "statement-based" MCQ angle.

    New military leadership (mid-2026)

    A near-complete change of guard occurred in mid-2026: CDS General Raja Subramani (from 31 May 2026), COAS General Dhiraj Seth (from 30 June 2026), CNS Vice Admiral Krishna Swaminathan (from 31 May 2026, the 27th Chief of the Naval Staff); CAS Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh (in office since 30 September 2024). The President, Droupadi Murmu, remains Supreme Commander. Leadership-change questions are a staple of AFCAT/NDA current-awareness sections — learn this table.

    Indigenisation milestones

    DRDO's Kusha long-range surface-to-air missile had its maiden flight test in July 2026 — designed to counter aircraft, missiles and UAVs. India signed a ₹1,943-crore lease for two MQ-9B Sea Guardian drones. Defence exports continue to rise (80+ buyer countries; the stated goal is ₹50,000 crore in annual exports by 2029). The two Defence Industrial Corridors (UP and Tamil Nadu) and iDEX startup challenges remain the policy backbone of Atmanirbharta.

    Exercises and national developments in the news

    Yudh Abhyas 22 (September 2026) — India-US Army exercise held for the first time in a two-theatre format: desert/precision-fires phase at Mahajan Field Firing Ranges, Rajasthan, then high-altitude phase at Auli, Uttarakhand. On the national front: the Agnipath/Agniveer scheme (launched 2022) continues as the sole entry route for soldiers below officer rank; AFCAT 2 2026 results were declared on 9 September 2026 (379 vacancies); the new personal Play Store developer account route for defence apps reflects the broader push for indigenous defence-tech entrepreneurship. Also track: the 2026 Defence Acquisition Procedure updates and any Rafale/MRFA and Project-75I submarine headlines. National current affairs with defence overlap: the Agnipath scheme's ongoing Agniveer intakes across Army, Navy, and Air Force; the push for women in combat roles (women officers now in permanent commission across streams, women Agniveers in all three services); and border infrastructure headlines — new bridges, tunnels, and the Vibrant Villages programme along the LAC. These are the "second-order" current-affairs questions that separate toppers.

    Revision method: for every item above, frame the MCQ yourself — who, what, where, when, how much. Question-setters convert exactly these facts ("Operation Sindoor was launched in response to which attack?") into options, so drill them as flashcards.

    The September 2026 exercise season

    September 2026 was the busiest joint-exercise month in recent memory — and each drill is a distinct MCQ set. Yudh Abhyas 2026 (22nd edition, from 15 September) ran in a two-theatre format: precision-fires and drone-heavy manoeuvres at the Mahajan Field Firing Ranges, Rajasthan, followed by high-altitude operations at Auli, Uttarakhand, with indigenous stars like the Pinaka multi-launch rocket system and Dhanush gun in the live firing. Tarang Shakti 2026 (scheduled 26 September–12 October at Jodhpur, theme "Power in Partnership") was the IAF's flagship multilateral air exercise — with the F-35 Lightning II's first tactical participation in an Indian-hosted drill as the headline fact, and foreign contingents including Australia, the US, UAE, France, Germany, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Nomadic Elephant 2026 (18th edition, 21 September–3 October at Pithoragarh) paired India with Mongolia (45 personnel each) for counter-insurgency training in semi-urban and mountainous terrain. Examination tip: learn each exercise as a tuple — edition + partner + location + dates + headline system.

    DAC's September 2026 mega-approvals and what they buy

    On 7 September 2026, the Defence Acquisition Council accorded Acceptance of Necessity for proposals worth about ₹1.10 lakh crore, with roughly 98% to be sourced from Indian industry — the single biggest Atmanirbhar signal of the year. For the Army: CBRN reconnaissance vehicles, high-mobility vehicles, mounted mortar systems, advanced light helicopters, mechanised trawls and Sarvatra bridging systems. For the Navy: Arudhra active electronically scanned array radars (to replace ageing Air Route Surveillance Radars at naval air stations) and marine gas turbines. For the Air Force: an advanced jammer system for electronic warfare and the Defence Forces Secure Access Card (DEFSAC) — an RFID-enabled smart card replacing paper ID cards and passes. The same month, the MoD signed a ₹586-crore Make-II contract with Accurate Industrial Controls for Auxiliary Power Units for T-72 and T-90 tanks — the APUs power fire-control systems, firing circuits and gun stabilisation when the main engine is off. These items convert directly into "match the following" and statement-based questions.

    Leadership, restructuring and records in 2026

    The mid-2026 change of guard reshaped the top table: CDS General Raja Subramani (31 May 2026), COAS General Dhiraj Seth (30 June 2026), CNS Vice Admiral Krishna Swaminathan (31 May 2026, 27th Naval Chief), CAS Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh (since September 2024), with Lt Gen Sandeep Jain as Vice Chief of the Army Staff and Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit as Vice Chief of the Air Staff. Structurally, the Army is raising Bhairav light commando battalions (~250 personnel each) for hybrid warfare and high-tempo operations, and every infantry battalion is to raise its own Ashni drone platoon — the clearest sign that drone warfare lessons from Operation Sindoor are being institutionalised. On the export front, FY2025-26 defence exports hit a record ₹38,424 crore (up ~62.7%, 145 exporters, 80+ buyer countries), with the BrahMos as the flagship export and deliveries underway to the Philippines. In space security, ISRO's Advanced Radar Research Centre under Project NETRA is coming up at Chandrapur near Guwahati to track objects in orbit. On the exam calendar: NDA & NA (II) 2026 was held on 13 September 2026 and AFCAT 2 2026 results were declared on 9 September 2026 (379 vacancies) — know the cycle, because notifications, exams and results are themselves asked as current affairs.

    11. SSB Interview & Psychology Tests: The Complete Breakdown

    The Services Selection Board (SSB) is a five-day personality assessment — not a knowledge test. Three independent assessors (Psychologist, Group Testing Officer, Interviewing Officer) each evaluate the same 15 Officer-Like Qualities (OLQs) and must agree before you are recommended. Roughly: planning & organising, effective intelligence, reasoning ability, power of expression, social adaptability, cooperation, sense of responsibility, initiative, self-confidence, decision-making speed, ability to influence the group, liveliness, determination, courage, and stamina. Everything below serves these fifteen.

    Day 1: Screening (PPDT + OIR)

    Screening eliminates 60–70% of candidates. OIR (Officer Intelligence Rating): two booklets of verbal/non-verbal reasoning — practise until 40+ is routine. PPDT (Picture Perception & Description Test): a hazy picture for 30 seconds, 4 minutes to write a story (hero, action, outcome), then 30-second narration and group discussion. Rules: make your hero you (same age/sex), show positive purposeful action, and in discussion, speak early, support others' good points, and merge ideas rather than dominating. If screened out, you go home the same day — so PPDT preparation is non-negotiable.

    Day 2: Psychology tests

    TAT (Thematic Apperception Test): 11 pictures + 1 blank slide, 30 seconds to view and 4 minutes to write each story. Write 11 tight stories: clear hero, a problem, constructive action, successful outcome. The blank slide tests imagination under zero stimulus — carry one ready-made positive story. WAT (Word Association Test): 60 words, 15 seconds each — write the first positive, action-oriented sentence that comes to mind. Never write negative, philosophical, or evasive sentences ("War is bad" fails; "War demands supreme sacrifice, soldiers embrace it" passes). SRT (Situation Reaction Test): 60 situations in 30 minutes — respond with decisive, resourceful, socially responsible action. Incomplete attempts hurt less than blank ones; attempt all 60. SD (Self-Description): what parents, teachers, friends think of you, plus your own assessment and areas to improve — must be consistent with your PIQ and interview answers.

    Days 3–4: GTO tasks

    Group Discussion (GD): two topics, ~20 minutes each — initiate with facts, build on others, conclude. Group Planning Exercise (GPE): study the model, write your plan (5–10 min), then discuss to converge on a group plan; nominate one member to present. Progressive/ Half/ Command/ Final Group Tasks (PGT, HGT, CT, FGT): outdoor obstacle courses with planks, ropes, and drums — rules: no touching out-of-bounds (coloured) areas, the helping material can't touch the ground. Be the candidate who holds the plank, gives the idea, and carries the load — ideas plus physical contribution. Individual Obstacles (IO): 10 obstacles, 3 minutes — attempt all, repeat high-scoring ones. Lecturette: 3 minutes on a topic picked from 4 cards after 3 minutes' prep — structure: intro, 3 points, conclusion. Command Task: you are the commander — call subordinates by name/chest number, give clear instructions, stay calm when the GTO increases pressure.

    The Personal Interview (PI)

    A 30–45 minute conversation built on your PIQ (Personal Information Questionnaire) — the form you fill on arrival. Every hobby, achievement, marksheet dip, and family detail will be questioned. Prepare: complete academics (favourite subjects with depth), current affairs with opinions, why you want to join (service-specific, not generic patriotism), backup plan honesty, and 5–6 detailed stories demonstrating OLQs from your real life. Technique: SAR (Situation-Action-Result) answers, short and specific; never bluff — "I don't know, sir/ma'am" beats a fabricated answer. Dress formally, sit upright, and let the interviewer lead.

    Day 5: Conference and the classic mistakes

    Each candidate appears before the full board for ~1 minute; borderline cases get rapid-fire questions. Results are announced the same day; recommended candidates stay for medicals. Mistakes that sink candidates: memorised "book" TAT stories (assessors spot coaching-centre templates instantly), dominating the GD, freezing in GTO tasks, contradicting your PIQ, negative WAT sentences, and projecting desperation. The single best preparation: live a life that demonstrates OLQs — play team sports, lead something, read the news daily, know yourself. SSB rewards genuine personality, not performance.

    12. Physical Fitness & Medical Standards

    Fitness doesn't earn marks in the written exam, but it decides everything after: the GTO's outdoor tasks, the academy's training, and the medical board. Candidates fail medicals every year for preventable reasons — this chapter tells you the standards and how to meet them months before your SSB.

    What the SSB physically demands

    There is no timed run at the SSB itself, but the GTO outdoor tasks (PGT, HGT, FGT, Individual Obstacles, Command Task) need real upper-body strength, grip, agility, and stamina. Target benchmarks before you report: 1.6 km in under 6:30, 10+ pull-ups, 40+ push-ups, and comfort with rope climbing, balancing, and jumping. The academies are stricter: NDA's first-term routine includes daily PT, swimming, horse riding, and cross-country runs — arrive unfit and you risk injury or relegation. Build over 12+ weeks: run 3–4x/week (one interval session, one long slow run), bodyweight strength 3x/week, one rest day minimum, and increase weekly volume by no more than ~10%.

    Medical standards: the essentials

    Standards are laid down in the official notifications and applied by the Special Medical Board (SMB), with Appeal (AMB) and Review (RMB) boards available. Key parameters (approximate — always check your entry's current notification): Height: minimum ~157 cm (men) / ~152 cm (women), with relaxations for some regions; weight proportionate to height and age per the official chart (±10% tolerance typically). Vision: uncorrected 6/6 and 6/9 correctable to 6/6 for flying branches (NDA/Air Force flying has the strictest limits); LASIK/PRK surgery is permitted for most ground-duty entries only after one year with conditions — not permitted for flying branches. Hearing: normal; dental: minimum 14 dental points; blood pressure within normal limits; no chronic skin disease, no flat feet or knock knees beyond limits, full joint mobility, and no history of asthma/epilepsy.

    Common rejection causes (and fixes)

    The most frequent medical rejections are overweight/underweight, myopia beyond limits, ear wax or perforated eardrums, hydrocele/varicocele, pilonidal sinus, knock knees/flat feet, carrying angle of elbow, deviated nasal septum affecting breathing, and tattoos (permitted only on inner forearm for most entries, with tribal-tradition exceptions). Many are fixable: get a pre-medical checkup 3–4 months before your SSB — a civil surgeon or ex-serviceman doctor can spot wax, weight, vision, and minor surgical issues in one visit. Temporary rejection (e.g., overweight, wax, minor surgery needed) gives you ~42 days to fix it and reappear before the Appeal Medical Board; permanent rejection (e.g., colour blindness for flying, chronic conditions) ends that entry's medical route.

    The 12-week pre-SSB fitness protocol

    Weeks 1–4 (base): 3 easy runs/week (20–30 min), bodyweight circuit (push-ups, squats, planks, pull-up negatives), daily stretching. Weeks 5–8 (build): add intervals (400 m repeats), increase pull-ups/push-ups volume, add rope-climb practice and obstacle-style play (monkey bars, vaulting). Weeks 9–12 (peak): timed 1.6 km weekly, full IO-style circuit practice, one mock GTO-style group activity with friends. Throughout: sleep 7–8 hours, eat protein at every meal, hydrate, and never train through sharp pain — shin splints and stress fractures from crash training end more SSB dreams than laziness does. Get running shoes fitted, not fashionable. Swimming deserves special mention: NDA training includes compulsory swimming, and non-swimmers struggle badly in the first term — learn basic freestyle and treading water before you join. Likewise, if you have never ridden a horse or done a rope climb, one introductory session removes the fear factor that freezes candidates in GTO tasks.

    Bottom line: written exam gets you to the SSB; fitness gets you through the GTO tasks and the medical board. Start the 12-week protocol the day you start written preparation, not the day you get your call-up letter.

    Nothing here is saved between visits — revise in one sitting, and bookmark this page to come back.
